evidence.auth_model: ACP itself defines no fixed auth mechanism; auth is delegated per-agent-implementation. Per docs (agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/schema, "Authentication"): the Agent advertises `authMethods` (each an `AuthMethod` with `id`, `name`, optional `description`) during `initialize`, and if a session cannot be created without auth the Agent returns an `auth_required` error and the Client calls `authenticate` with a chosen method id. Two method shapes exist: "Agent handles authentication itself through `authenticate`. This is the default when no `type` is specified" (`type` omitted/"agent"), or `type: "terminal"` where the "Client runs the configured agent program as a separate interactive process, without passing this method to `authenticate`" — i.e. the client shells out to the underlying agent CLI's own interactive login. This terminal path is exactly how the known official adapters bind ACP to native CLI logins (e.g. `claude-code-acp` delegates to the Claude Code CLI's own subscription login; `codex-acp`-style adapters delegate to Codex/ChatGPT login) rather than ACP mandating an API key.

evidence.interface: ACP is a JSON-RPC 2.0 wire protocol, not an SDK you call as a library function per se, though official runtime SDKs (Rust `agent-client-protocol`, TypeScript `@agentclientprotocol/sdk`, Python, Kotlin, Java) implement it. Local agents run as editor subprocesses communicating over stdio; remote agents (still "work in progress" per docs) speak HTTP/WebSocket. Core methods: `initialize` (capability/version negotiation), `authenticate`, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, `session/cancel`, `session/update` (server->client notifications carrying structured tool-call/message events), `session/request_permission`, plus terminal methods (`terminal/create`, `terminal/output`, `terminal/wait_for_exit`, `terminal/kill`, `terminal/release`). This is a headless, event-driven control-plane interface between an editor/client and any coding agent.
evidence.isolation_model: No isolation/sandbox is defined by ACP itself. Tool execution (including terminal commands) runs "within the Client's environment": the Client process owns the actual OS process, working directory and lifecycle (create/output/wait/kill/release), while the Agent only requests actions and receives structured status back. There is no per-session container, VM or worktree concept in the protocol; any sandboxing, per-worktree isolation or "deterministic code owns the effects" guarantee has to come from the specific Client or Agent implementation, not from ACP.
evidence.worker_features: ACP supports concurrent/queued session management (session/new, session/load, session/cancel), resumable sessions via `sessionCapabilities.resume` (reconnect without full history replay) or `loadSession` (full replay), custom tool-call reporting with kind/status/content (text, images, resource blocks, diffs, live terminal output), explicit MCP server wiring per session (stdio/HTTP/SSE), and a permission-request round trip (session/request_permission) so a client can gate risky actions. There is no built-in multi-worker/fan-out orchestration primitive in the protocol itself — dispatch/parallelism is left to the Client or Agent implementation.
evidence.structured_events: session/update notifications are the structured-event channel: they carry tool-call lifecycle updates (toolCallId, human-readable title, kind: read/edit/execute/fetch, status: pending/in_progress/completed/failed), diff content for file edits, live terminal output tied to a terminalId, and agent message/thought chunks. Combined with the JSON Schema published under schema/v1 and schema/v2 in this repo, these events are machine-parseable and versioned, not just log text.

evidence.summary: codex-acp (agentclientprotocol/codex-acp) is an actively maintained, Apache-2.0-licensed, npm-published stdio Agent Client Protocol (ACP) server that wraps OpenAI Codex's App Server, translating ACP JSON-RPC requests into Codex operations and mapping Codex's own events (shell, file-change, permission, MCP tool call, reasoning, plan, subagent, async-task, etc.) back to any ACP-speaking client (e.g. Zed, JetBrains AIR). It authenticates exactly the way the incumbent `openai/codex` CLI does — ChatGPT/OpenAI login, or an API key, or an opted-in custom gateway — so it fits C1 cleanly. It adds a standardized, capability-negotiated protocol surface (native subagent sessions, background async terminal tasks, structured permission-presentation metadata, session/load resumability) beyond what raw `codex exec` output parsing offers, which is its candidate value versus the incumbent. Evidence quality is solid (weekly releases through 2026-09-15, CI + a separate e2e workflow, real unit tests under src/__tests__ despite no top-level tests/ dir, and a verified Apache-2.0 LICENSE file that contradicts GitHub's own NOASSERTION license-detector flag). evidence.worker_features: Model, reasoning-effort, fast-mode, approval-mode, and sandbox-mode configuration is exposed; an opt-in 'AIR recommended config values' capability surfaces concrete recommended model/reasoning-effort values. Native ACP subagent sessions provide separate child histories and root-routed permissions/elicitations (bilateral capability negotiation; legacy tool-call fallback otherwise; `session/load` reconstructs the child tree from Codex history with defined orphan/timeout/shutdown/notFound fallback semantics, diverging from the draft RFD's 'unknown outcome' rule). Background terminal tasks let a shell command keep running after its initiating tool call returns, surfaced via the AIR async-task extension with spawn/state-update/stop lifecycle and a `showInTranscript:false` flag so the originating command card (not a duplicate) owns the output; a provider restart or app-server exit resolves outstanding tasks to `failed`/reassigns control. evidence.summary: GitHub's official MCP server (Go, MIT, 33,125 stars as of 2026-09-22) exposes GitHub's REST/GraphQL/code-security surface as MCP tools, either as a local stdio binary/Docker container or as GitHub's hosted remote HTTP server, with per-toolset enable/disable, read-only mode, and a Copilot-coding-agent dispatch tool (create_pull_request_with_copilot, assign_copilot_to_issue). It overlaps this project's existing `gh` CLI usage for PR/issue/Actions work and is judged keep_but_compare by all three source judges, not adopted outright.
evidence.interface: Local mode: a Go binary/Docker image run as `github-mcp-server stdio` (stdio JSON-RPC MCP transport), or built from cmd/github-mcp-server. Remote mode: hosted Streamable-HTTP MCP server at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ (docs/streamable-http.md, docs/remote-server.md). Tool surface is grouped into toolsets (repos, issues, pull_requests, actions, code_security, context, stargazers, etc., README ~535-585) selectable via --toolsets/GITHUB_TOOLSETS, plus a --read-only/GITHUB_READ_ONLY flag that strips all write tools (README 479, 1645-1656). No dedicated SDK beyond the standard MCP client contract; integration is "point an MCP host at this server," not a Python/TS SDK import.
evidence.auth_model: Dual: (1) OAuth login — README: "Log in with OAuth (no token to create or store). On github.com the official image already includes the app credentials, so you provide none yourself: it runs a browser-based login on first use and keeps the resulting token in memory only." Docker needs a fixed loopback callback port (127.0.0.1:8085) for the browser callback; headless/device-code fallback and bring-your-own OAuth/GitHub App are documented in docs/oauth-login.md (required for GHES/ghe.com). (2) Personal Access Token — README: "Prefer a token? You can still authenticate with a GitHub Personal Access Token by setting GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN instead (it takes precedence over OAuth)." Remote server supports both OAuth (VS Code 1.101+, Claude Desktop, etc., via host-configured GitHub App/OAuth App) and PAT-as-bearer-header. Non-interactive stdio deployments can use GitHub App auth (docs/github-app-auth.md) instead. No separate paid API key of any kind is required — the strongest C1 fit in the slice, matching all three judges' claim.
evidence.isolation_model: No sandboxing of its own: the server is a thin API proxy (local process or Docker container, or GitHub's hosted remote instance) that calls the GitHub API with the caller's token/PAT scope. A worktree or task can "own" it only via toolset/read-only flags and PAT scope, not process isolation — it never executes user code, it manipulates GitHub state directly, so it has no sandboxed filesystem/execution boundary of the kind C3 asks about. Docker mode gives OS-level container isolation for the server process itself, not per-task/per-worktree separation of GitHub-side effects.
evidence.worker_features: No native agent/dispatch runtime of its own beyond exposing GitHub's Copilot coding agent as callable tools: assign_copilot_to_issue, assign_copilot_to_issue_with_intent (records a pending assignment or launches the agent; README 744-749), and create_pull_request_with_copilot ("Perform task with GitHub Copilot coding agent", README 1608). These delegate execution to GitHub's own hosted Copilot coding-agent service rather than to a locally controlled worker/session model. No resumable-session or custom-tool-hosting mechanism beyond standard MCP; --toolsets is the main scoping primitive for reducing context/attack surface per deployment.
evidence.structured_events: Tool responses are standard MCP structured JSON-RPC results (e.g. field-resolution errors return "a structured error", README 1173). No evidence in the README of a distinct structured event/telemetry stream beyond individual tool call/response pairs; the repo tree shows a pkg/observability package and docs/error-handling.md that likely cover this in more depth but were not read for this packet — recorded as an open gap.

evidence.auth_model: Server-side: FastMCP ships built-in OAuth providers, including a `GitHubProvider`, plus documented support for Google, Azure, AWS "and most traditional enterprise identity systems" via an `OAuthProxy` pattern for IdPs lacking Dynamic Client Registration (DCR), and `RemoteAuthProvider`/DCR-native support for WorkOS AuthKit and Descope. Token verification is via `JWTVerifier` (validates against known issuers/audiences). No FastMCP-vendor API key is required — the project itself has no paid API/vendor key; server operators instead configure credentials for whichever IdP (GitHub/Google/etc.) they choose, and a separate `fastmcp auth`/`login`/`whoami`/`logout` CLI surface manages OAuth documents for the FastMCP Cloud account layer. Source: https://gofastmcp.com/servers/auth/authentication (source_review, WebFetch summary, quotes above) and https://gofastmcp.com/cli/overview (source_review).

claims.claim: 27,865 stars, Apache-2.0 license, not archived, pushed 2026-09-22 (0-day push relative to evidence date), default branch main.
Latest release is v4.0.5 'No Country for Loose Ints', published 2026-09-17T17:38:11Z, with a security regression test and a validation-coercion fix noted in the changelog.
Repository has a top-level tests/ directory with subdirectories including server, client, cli, conformance, integration_tests, telemetry, tasks, fs, apps — i.e. a real, structured test suite.

CI is configured via GitHub Actions workflows including run-tests.yml, run-static.yml, run-schema-crash-test.yml, run-upgrade-checks.yml, deploy-docs.yml, and multiple publish-*.yml package-release workflows.

README states 'FastMCP 1.0 was incorporated into the official MCP Python SDK in 2024' and claims 'some version of FastMCP powers 70% of MCP servers across all languages' and 'downloaded a million times a day' — self-reported adoption claims, not independently verified.

FastMCP has three pillars: Servers, Apps (interactive UIs rendered in the conversation), and Clients (connect to any MCP server, local or remote, programmatic or CLI) — i.e. it is a superset framework, not just a server SDK.

Auth: built-in OAuth providers (GitHubProvider explicit; Google/Azure/AWS via OAuthProxy for non-DCR IdPs; WorkOS AuthKit and Descope for DCR-native IdPs) plus JWTVerifier for bearer-token validation; no FastMCP-vendor API key required for the OSS server framework.

evidence.summary: FastMCP (PrefectHQ/fastmcp) is a mature, actively maintained Apache-2.0 Python framework for authoring MCP servers, clients and "Apps" (in-conversation UIs), whose v1.0 was folded into the official modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk in 2024. It has 27,865 stars, a real tests/ directory (server, client, cli, conformance, integration_tests, telemetry, tasks, fs, apps subdirs), CI via multiple GitHub Actions workflows (run-tests.yml, run-static.yml, run-schema-crash-test.yml, run-upgrade-checks.yml, plus release/publish and triage-bot workflows), and a latest release v4.0.5 published 2026-09-17 with the repo pushed as recently as 2026-09-22. It requires no vendor API key for local/OSS server use; it ships built-in OAuth provider support (GitHubProvider explicit; Google/Azure/AWS via OAuthProxy; WorkOS AuthKit/Descope via DCR) and JWTVerifier bearer-token validation, and a `fastmcp` CLI (run/dev/install/inspect/call/discover/generate-cli/project) plus a separate, apparently optional, FastMCP Cloud account layer (login/whoami/logout/auth). Its central strategic problem for this catalog is direct overlap with the already-selected modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk for authoring MCP servers; all three shortlist judges converge on keep_but_compare with the same named comparison (build one project MCP server both ways and compare boilerplate/auth/test ergonomics), and none of the extra claims (CLI headless mode structured events, resumable sessions) were verifiable from the docs pages actually reachable in this packet.

evidence.summary: Snyk Agent Scan is a Python CLI (`snyk-agent-scan`) that discovers agent harnesses, MCP server configs and agent skills on a machine and scans them for prompt injection, tool poisoning/shadowing, toxic flows, malicious skill code, secret handling and other supply-chain risks, sending redacted component data to the Snyk Agent Scan analysis API (or a self-hosted Snyk Evo instance for fleet/background mode).
evidence.interface: CLI only (`snyk-agent-scan scan|inspect|help [CONFIG_FILE...]`), distributed via `uvx snyk-agent-scan@latest`/`@0.5.17` (PyPI package `snyk-agent-scan`) or standalone signed binaries per-OS/arch from GitHub Releases (with SBOM, checksums, GPG-signed checksums). It is a security scanner over MCP/skill configs, not an SDK for building MCP servers or agents, and not itself an MCP server (source_review: README Quick Start / CLI Parameters sections).
evidence.auth_model: Requires a Snyk account and API token set as `SNYK_TOKEN` env var, obtained from https://app.snyk.io/account (source_review: README 'Before using either option' steps 1-2, quoted: 'Sign up at Snyk and get an API token ... Set the token as an environment variable before running any scan: export SNYK_TOKEN=your-api-token-here'). Background/MDM 'push-key' fleet mode reports to a Snyk Evo instance and is contact-sales gated. No use of Claude Code, Codex/ChatGPT, GitHub or Google native login is documented anywhere in the README or file tree; this is a separate paid Snyk credential, which C1 records as a penalty rather than an exclusion.
evidence.isolation_model: Runs as a local process against the caller's discovered agent config files; scanning MCP configs can execute stdio server commands and make outbound network requests to configured remote MCP URLs. The README explicitly recommends running scans "inside a sandbox (Docker container, VM, or disposable environment)" for untrusted configs, gates server contact behind an interactive per-server y/n consent prompt by default (declined servers get `user_declined` and are never contacted), and only skips consent for background/push-key fleet scans, which still do not start stdio servers unless `--dangerously-run-mcp-servers` is passed (source_review: README 'Security Warning' and 'Interactive Consent for MCP Servers' sections). It also applies SSRF-style guards, refusing remote MCP requests to link-local/cloud-metadata ranges (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10, fd00:ec2::254, 100.100.100.200), not following redirects, though it notes a DNS-rebinding window between initial DNS validation and connection time (source_review: README, same section). This is caller-provided process isolation guidance (Docker/VM), not a sandbox the tool itself provides.
evidence.worker_features: Not an orchestration/dispatch SDK; "worker" features here are scanner concepts: two run modes (interactive foreground Scan Mode producing a one-shot report, and Background/MDM Mode that scans on regular intervals and reports centrally to Snyk Evo for fleet-wide monitoring). No custom-tool/dispatch or multi-agent worker API is documented (source_review: README 'Scanner Capabilities' section).
evidence.structured_events: v0.6+ emits a "risk-based" scored report format against a versioned analysis API (2026-07-10); v0.5.x emits an issue-code based format against the 2025-09-02 API. Both output schemas are explicitly marked experimental/unstable: README quotes "The raw output of this CLI — including risk indicator names, scores, field names, and response structure — is experimental and may change without notice between releases. We do not recommend building production workflows that depend on specific CLI output fields or risk names" (source_review: README banner). No mention of resumable sessions or a documented event-stream/webhook contract for the local CLI itself; background mode's reporting contract into Snyk Evo is not detailed in this repo's README.

risks: Requires a separate Snyk account and paid/free-tier API token (SNYK_TOKEN) rather than any native Claude/Codex/GitHub/Google login — an external credential dependency and potential cost/ToS surface (agreeing to Snyk's Agent Scan terms of use is required per the README).

Scanning MCP configs can execute stdio server commands and issue outbound network requests as a side effect of the scan itself; interactive consent and SSRF guards mitigate but do not eliminate this (README notes an unresolved DNS-rebinding window between validation and connection time).

Component data (agent details, MCP server configs/signatures, tool names/descriptions, skill content) is sent to Snyk's analysis API for scoring; secrets are redacted before transmission per the README, but this is still third-party data egress for anyone running the scan against this project's configs unless self-hosted Evo is used.

v0.5.x is stated as 'planned for deprecation', so any integration should target v0.6+.

evidence.summary: Supergateway is an MIT-licensed TypeScript CLI (npx-run, also Docker/GHCR images) that bridges a local stdio MCP server to network transports (SSE, WebSocket, Streamable HTTP) and the reverse (SSE/Streamable-HTTP remote server exposed locally as stdio). v4.0.0 (2026-09-20, 2 days before this evidence pull) is the current stable release, requires Node 20+, and the release notes claim a 36/36-job six-hour soak across Node 20/22/24/26 on Linux/macOS/Windows plus 100% per-file coverage (release-notes claim, not independently reproduced here). The repo carries a large tests/ directory (120+ *.test.ts files covering session lifecycle, SSE/WS/HTTP edges, header redaction, child-process ownership/reaping, etc.) and five GitHub Actions workflows (tests, npm-publish, docker-publish, release-soak, release-soak-lane).
evidence.interface: CLI only, invoked via `npx -y supergateway <flags>` (or Docker: `docker run supercorp/supergateway ...`). Core modes read from README: `--stdio "command"` (stdio server to bridge out), `--outputTransport stdio|sse|ws|streamableHttp`, `--sse URL` / `--streamableHttp URL` (bridge a remote server back to local stdio), plus `--port`, `--baseUrl`, `--ssePath`, `--messagePath`, `--streamableHttpPath`, `--stateful`, `--sessionTimeout`, `--cors`, `--healthEndpoint`, `--logLevel`. No importable SDK/library surface is documented in the README beyond the CLI binary (`dist/index.js`); `package.json` depends internally on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.30.0` and companion `@modelcontextprotocol/{client,node,server}@2.0.0` packages.
evidence.auth_model: No native login of its own. For outbound connections to a remote SSE/Streamable-HTTP MCP server it is bridging, the README documents `--oauth2Bearer "some-access-token"` ("Adds an `Authorization` header with the provided Bearer token") and generic `--header "x-user-id: 123"` (repeatable) for auth headers ("This is useful for authentication"). These are user-supplied tokens/headers passed straight through, not an OAuth or account-login flow the tool manages itself. No mention of Claude Code, Codex/ChatGPT, GitHub, or Google sign-in anywhere in the README, release bodies, or package.json reviewed.
evidence.isolation_model: Runs as a single OS process per invocation, launching the wrapped stdio MCP server as a child process; no built-in sandbox/container isolation of its own beyond normal process boundaries (Docker images are provided as an external isolation option, not gateway-internal sandboxing). Per-worktree/per-worker isolation would come from the caller running one `supergateway` instance (own port/child process) per worktree — the README documents no shared global daemon or shared state across instances. `--stateful` mode holds server-side session state (30-minute idle expiry per v4.0.0 release notes) scoped to that one running gateway process.
evidence.worker_features: No agent/worker dispatch, task queue, or multi-agent orchestration features. It is a transport bridge only: one stdio MCP server in, one or more network-transport clients out (or vice versa). `multiClientSse.test.ts` in the test suite suggests multiple SSE clients can attach to one bridged stdio server.
evidence.structured_events: Relays MCP JSON-RPC protocol messages/notifications between transports (stdio to SSE/WS/Streamable HTTP); v4.0.0 changelog specifically claims fixes to notification/reply delivery and progress-notification ordering. Not a general "structured agent event" or telemetry stream — it is MCP wire-protocol passthrough, evidenced by test files named modernProtocol.test.ts, protocolVersionMatrix.test.ts, statefulNotificationRouting.test.ts.
evidence.tests_and_ci: Confirmed via gh api repos/supercorp-ai/supergateway/contents/tests (120+ *.test.ts files, node --test runner per package.json) and gh api .../contents/.github/workflows (5 workflow files: tests.yaml, npm-publish.yaml, docker-publish.yaml, release-soak.yaml, release-soak-lane.yaml). has_ci/has_tests_dir claims from the shortlist reasons are corroborated by directory listings.
